title: American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
content_c:
American ranchers wrestle with soaring costs - and their loyalty to Trump
- Published
Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year.
In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines.
Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed.
With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000.
On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year.
Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold.
The cattle market tanked immediately.
'It felt like a betrayal'
"So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry."
"It just felt like a betrayal," she said.
Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain.
That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances.
Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race.
Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months.
The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices.
And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive.
Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle.
"All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas.
Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing.
Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own.
The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry.
But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning.
"Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head.
Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day.
"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.
That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.
An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".
- What are the US midterms? A simple guide 
  - Published6 days ago
- The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope 
  - Published5 days ago
Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.
Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.
But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

"It really makes a guy think," he said.
A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left.
But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market.
"People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said.
'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business'
Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall.
"The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said.
"I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit."
Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago.
But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said.
He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House.
Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms.
But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate.
That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago.
Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper.
He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts.
That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry.
"Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News.
An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy".
Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical".
But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt.
"We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it."
But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction".
- What are the US midterms? A simple guide 
  - Published6 days ago
- The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope 
  - Published5 days ago
Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things".
But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed.
"Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste."
Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions.
"I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said.
Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture."
Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said.
Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later.
But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter.
"It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in.
He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers.
"I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'"
Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state.
"They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore."
All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on.
On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction.
Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - don not pause for politics.
Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude.
"People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it."

title: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
content_c:
Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street.
Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had.
Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote.
The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote.
A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum.
The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts.
It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election.
The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded.
Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right.
Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.
Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.
“I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”
He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia.
“One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.”
He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”
The UK is developing a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt hostile state information campaigns aimed at undermining British democracy. Downing Street said it was working with Germany on a new partnership to counter hybrid threats, including hostile activities that threaten both countries’ security and prosperity.
A spokesperson said: “National security is the first duty of any government – we are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.
“We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies.
“We will continue to leave no stone unturned in our efforts to protect the UK from harm.”
Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.

title: Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
content_c:
Germany rejects Trump demand, 'fully supports' Zelenskyy
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 12, 2026
What you need to know
This blog is now closed. It was a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 10, and Sunday, October 11.
- Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin 'fully supports' Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
- The gesture of solidarity came in response to Donald Trump's calls for new leadership in Ukraine
- Friedrich Merz's CDU gathers for leadership meeting addressing electoral free fall
- The German government has said it will continue working with EU partners on Russia sanctions
- Ex-Chancellor Gerhard Schröder faces criticism for attending Putin's birthday
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Thank you for reading
Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog. We will back with more news in a fresh blog on Monday.
Söder stands by Merz as chancellor
Bavarian premier Markus Söder has affirmed his support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz amid growing speculation about a change of federal leadership.
Söder leads the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
"Friedrich Merz is chancellor and will remain chancellor," Söder said in a television interview on Sunday night.
He added that a change of chancellor is something that only occurs under "extreme" conditions.
In the same interview Söder went on to endorse Bavaria state parliament president Ilse Aigner to be Germany's next president after Frank-Walter Steinmeier's term ends in March.
He called her "a highly suitable candidate," although she has not declared any intention to run in next year's presidential election.
Deutsche Bank CEO: Political extremism putting off foreign investors
Christian Sewing, CEO of Deutsche Bank, Germany's biggest, warned that the growing strength of both the far right and the far left is spooking foreign investors.
Sewing told the tabloid Bild that recent election victories for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and post-communist Left Party "pose a significant risk for Germany and should not be downplayed."
The Deutsche Bank boss said it mattered little that the elections were on the state and local level. "You can't expect a foreign investor to immediately draw a distinction between a state government and Germany as a whole," he said.
"It's seen as Germany as a whole and I think that from an investor's point of view, that's understandable."
Some economists say the AfD is creating an atmosphere that will drive away much needed skilled labor as well as foreign investors.
The Left Party, meanwhile, won victory in Berlin promising to expropriate residential property companies' holdings to lower housing costs in the German capital.
"Whether it's Saxony-Anhalt with the AfD or what's happening here in Berlin," said Sewing, "it's anything but conducive to economic growth. And it's anything but investment-friendly."
Sewing said Chancellor Friedrich Merz must get on with carrying out reforms and reviving the economy, saying, "That is the only response we have to the far-right and far-left extremists in this country."
Foreign Minister Wadephul: 'Germany fully supports' Zelenskyy
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Sunday made clear that Berlin stands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, rejecting US President Donald Trump's calls for his replacement.
Germany will "fully support the president as he carries out his difficult duties," said Wadephul at his party's two-day CDU leadership conference.
On Friday, after a long phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump announced a deal that would see sanctions on Russia eased dramatically and allow Moscow to export millions of barrels of diesel, thus pumping much needed cash into Russia's economy.
On Saturday, Trump called for Zelenskyy's removal and again sought to pin blame on the Ukrainian president — not his own Iran war — for high global oil prices.
Germany is the biggest EU donor to Ukraine, and an advocate for tighter sanctions and increased pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.
Berlin responded to Trump's oil scheme by stating that it would not be lifting any Russian sanctions.
On Sunday, Wadephul responded to the second point, making the case for "consistency and clarity" in terms of support for Ukraine.
"We don't need less pressure on Putin to force him to negotiate," said the German diplomat. "We need more," he added. "That is what this moment requires and that's what this government stands for."
Merz's CDU huddles to find way out of electoral free fall
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) will kick off a two-day leadership meeting on Sunday to plot a path out of the electoral crisis the party finds itself in after three dismal state elections.
The 25-member leadership meeting was called after the CDU — until now one of Germany's two largest popular parties — failed to even clear the 5% hurdle to enter Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state legislature. The stinging loss, which Merz himself described as "a disaster," represented the first time in the party's history that it was booted from a statehouse.
The CDU has been struggling to hold off the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and has been thrust into an identity crisis due to the rate at which it is losing voters to the party.
In one of the summer's other elections — in Saxony-Anhalt — the CDU dropped nearly 20 percentage points, getting clobbered by the AfD, which racked up over 40% of the vote.
This weekend's meeting is designed to address voter dissatisfaction with the CDU-led governing coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD), as well as looking at possible long-term solutions to the party's electoral death spiral.
Faced with this new electoral reality, leaders will reportedly look at the potential policy consequences of the party's losses, reconsidering whether to push on with much-needed reforms to the healthcare and retirement systems, for instance.
Party leaders will also grapple with the fundamental question of how to deal with the AfD in the long run, namely, whether to maintain the party's "firewall" policy rejecting any cooperation or to work with the anti-immigrant rightwing populists in hopes of remaining relevant.
Speaking with Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper ahead of the pow-wow, Hesse State Premier Boris Rhein said leadership, "has to deal with all of the issues that are important to everyday citizens: Cost of living, security, immigration and jobs."
This blog is on pause
We are pausing our coverage for now. Join us again on Sunday morning for more coverage of the German news and analysis.
Germany rejects proposed EU budget, calls for greater cuts
Germany swiftly rejected a proposed new budget for the European Union that was put forward on Saturday.
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, put forward a budget of €1.826 trillion ($2.046 trillion) for the next seven years — a reduction of around €159 billion compared to the European Commission's original proposal of nearly €1.985 trillion.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget cuts should go further.
"The size of the new proposal is no basis for an agreement," Merz said.
"The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the main burden of financing," he added.
Germany is the largest net contributor to the EU budget. It and other net contributors including the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland all want the next budget to be slashed by hundreds of billions of euros.
But the second-largest net contributor to the EU budget, France, has instead argued that the 27-member bloc needs a more generous budget in order to overcome new challenges.
'Ragebait' named Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year
The Langenscheidt publishing house on Saturday named "ragebait" as Germany's 2026 Youth Word of the Year during the Frankfurt Book Fair.
Ragebait is social media content designed to draw people in by making them angry with provocative claims, lies, or outrageous opinions, thereby driving up clicks and interactions.
Langenscheidt, Germany's best-selling dictionary publisher, organized an online poll with 1 million young people taking part in this year's competition.
Ragebait took 36.5% of the vote, with runners-up including the terms "peak," meaning the best of the best, and "crashout," meaning when someone loses their cool.
Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions
Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.
"The federal government has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
"The federal government remains committed to the decisions on sanctions against Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.
Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.
In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.
Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit
The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.
Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.
"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.
"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.
Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.
The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.
"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.
Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,
Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from Bonn.
The German government said European sanctions on Russia will continune unabated after the Trump administration paused US sanctions on Russian diesel yesterday.
And Germany's former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder is under fire after attending Vladimir Putin's birthday in Moscow.
Read on for this and more.
description: Germany's foreign minister has said Berlin is behind Ukraine's president and will keep pressuring Russia to end its war. Meanwhile, Deutsche Bank's CEO warned that political extremism is spooking investors. More on DW.

Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.
In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.
Ex-Chancellor Schröder criticized for Putin birthday visit
The appearance of Germany's Russia-friendly former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder at President Vladimir Putin's birthday party earlier this week has drawn criticism in Germany.
Franziska Brantner, the co-leader of Germany's Green party, called on Schröder's Social Democrats (SPD) to revisit revoking Schröder's party membership.
"Russia is now even attacking us in Germany with hybrid attacks. Schröder hasn't learned anything from this. A new approach needs to be put on the table," she told the Tagesspiegel newspaper.
"Schröder is celebrating Putin's birthday with him, while civilians in Ukraine are once again dying as a result of Russian attacks. This is politically unacceptable," said Brantner.
Anything less than expulsion from the party would be "a disastrous signal, not only to Ukraine but also to the people and their safety in our country," Brantner added.
The SPD's Hubertus Heil, who served as Germany's labor minister from 2018 to 2025, also criticized Schröder.
"The warm embrace between Schröder and Putin in Moscow deeply outrages and disturbs me," Heil told the Tagesspiegel.
Celebrating with a "dictator" whose "murderous imperialism causes horrific suffering every day" is "unjustifiable under any circumstances," he said.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands,
Schröder's business and personal ties to Russia have drawn controversy since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, but he fended off calls at the time by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from Bonn.
The German government said European sanctions on Russia will continune unabated after the Trump administration paused US sanctions on Russian diesel yesterday.
And Germany's former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder is under fire after attending Vladimir Putin's birthday in Moscow.
Read on for this and more.

title: Haftbefehl: Rapper steht laut seinem Bruder Capo unter »ärztlicher Aufsicht«
content_c:
Videobotschaft an Fans Rapper Haftbefehl steht laut seinem Bruder unter »ärztlicher Aufsicht«
Der Rapper Haftbefehl, 40, steht derzeit unter »ärztlicher Aufsicht und muss sich gerade voll und ganz auf seine Gesundheit konzentrieren«: Das sagte sein Bruder Cem Anhan, auch bekannt unter dem Künstlernamen Capo. Er veröffentlichte in der Nacht zu Montag auf dem Instagram- und TikTok-Account seines Bruders eine knapp einminütige Videobotschaft »im Namen der Familie«.
Behalten Sie den Überblick: Jeden Werktag gegen 18 Uhr beantworten SPIEGEL-Autorinnen und -Autoren die wichtigsten Fragen des Tages im Newsletter »Die Lage am Abend« – hintergründig, kompakt, kostenlos. Hier bestellen Sie Ihr News-Briefing als Mail.
Die Familie habe gemeinsam mit Haftbefehl entschieden, die angekündigten Konzerte des Rappers abzusagen. Er hätte im Oktober in Düsseldorf und Berlin auf der Bühne stehen sollen. »Wir wissen, dass viele jetzt enttäuscht sind und es tut uns umso mehr leid.« Die Familie bitte aber, diese Entscheidung zu respektieren »und ihm seine Zeit zu geben, die er jetzt braucht«.
Das Video von Cem Anhan ist der einzige Beitrag auf dem Instagramaccount von Haftbefehl. Er hat dort mehr als 1,2 Millionen Follower.
Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung.
Im Juni hatte Haftbefehl – der mit bürgerlichem Namen Aykut Anhan heißt – aus gesundheitlichen Gründen eine Pause angekündigt und sich aus der Öffentlichkeit zurückgezogen. Zuvor waren mehrere Termine kurzfristig abgesagt worden.
Zur Begründung hatte Haftbefehl auf die Netflix-Doku »Babo – Die Haftbefehl-Story« über ihn verwiesen, in der er offen über Drogensucht und die Folgen seines Kokainkonsums berichtet hatte (SPIEGEL-Autor Juan Moreno hat bei dem Dreh Regie geführt – wie er die Arbeit erlebte, lesen Sie hier ). Die dadurch entstandene Aufmerksamkeit habe ihn zusätzlich stark belastet, sagte Haftbefehl damals. »Deshalb brauche ich jetzt Ruhe und Zeit, um mich auf meine Gesundheit zu konzentrieren und wieder zu Kräften zu kommen.«

title: Selenskyj will Angriffe auf russische Raffinerien fortsetzen
content_c:
Trotz Trumps Drohungen Selenskyj setzt Angriffe auf russische Raffinerien fort
Nach Trumps Drohungen gegen den ukrainischen Präsidenten hat Selenskyj nun reagiert - und angekündigt, die Angriffe auf russische Ölraffinerien fortzusetzen. Ein Ende sei nur möglich, wenn auch Russland seine Attacken einstelle.
US-Präsident Donald Trump macht einen umstrittenen Dieseldeal mit Russland, fordert den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj zum Rücktritt auf und verlangt, dass die Ukraine ihre Angriffe auf russische Raffinerien einstellt. Nach den jüngsten Ereignissen dieses Wochenende sind die Beziehungen zwischen den USA und der Ukraine auf einem neuen Tiefpunkt angelangt.
Die Ukraine kündigte nun ihrerseits an, die Angriffe auf russische Ölraffinerien fortsetzen, ungeachtet des Drucks vonseiten Washingtons. Russland sei allein für den Krieg verantwortlich, erklärte Selenskyj.
Selenskyj: "Deeskalation muss auf Gegenseitigkeit beruhen"
"Die Ukraine wäre bereit, die Angriffe auf russische Ölraffinerien einzustellen, wenn Russland aufhört, unsere Energieinfrastruktur anzugreifen", schrieb Selenskyj auf der Plattform X. Die Angriffe auf die Energieinfrastruktur könnten umgehend beendet werden, aber Putin wolle das nicht. Jede Deeskalation müsse auf Gegenseitigkeit beruhen und durch echte Garantien untermauert werden.
Auch der ukrainische Außenminister Andrij Sybiha widersprach Trump und schrieb auf X, Selenskyj genieße die Unterstützung des ukrainischen Volkes und dieses habe das Recht, selbst zu entscheiden. "Äußerungen aus dem Ausland bestätigen nur, dass er seine Arbeit gut macht."
Trump hatte am Samstag gesagt, es sei an der Zeit, dass die Ukraine einen neuen Präsidenten bekomme. Er deutete an, dass Selenskyj nicht genug getan habe, um den Krieg zu beenden, und machte ihn für die hohen Dieselpreise in den USA verantwortlich.
Begonnen wurde der Krieg aber nicht von der Ukraine, sondern von Russland, das vor mehr als viereinhalb Jahren in das Nachbarland einmarschiert war. Kremlchef Wladimir Putin hat mehrfach Angebote für einen bedingungslosen Waffenstillstand abgelehnt. Auch spätere diplomatische Initiativen verliefen im Sande.
Diesel-Preis setzt Trump unter Druck
Zudem hatte Trump die Ukraine in den vergangenen Wochen mehrfach für eine weltweite Dieselknappheit verantwortlich gemacht. Allerdings waren die Treibstoffpreise aufgrund des Kriegs der USA gegen den Iran massiv in die Höhe geschnellt.
Der stark gestiegene Dieselpreis hat sich für Trumps Republikanische Partei im Vorfeld der im November anstehenden Zwischenwahlen zu einer politischen Belastung entwickelt, was sich auch am eingetrübten Verbrauchervertrauen ablesen lässt. Die oppositionellen Demokraten könnten davon profitieren und bei den Wahlen womöglich die Kontrolle über eines oder beide Häuser des Kongresses erlangen.
Vor diesem Hintergrund sehen manche Beobachterinnen und Beobachter das von Trump angekündigte Abkommen über Diesellieferungen aus Russland als taktisches Manöver. US-Finanzminister Scott Bessent verteidigte die umstrittene Vereinbarung mit Russland: "Es ist gut für die Amerikaner, die Dieselpreise zu senken", sagte er dem Sender Fox News.
Für Moskau ein weiterer Schritt zurück auf die Weltbühne
Analysten zufolge dürfte Trumps Deal mit Moskau allerdings kaum zu dauerhaft niedrigeren Kraftstoffpreisen führen. Denn die Liefermengen dürften weit unter dem Niveau liegen, das Russland üblicherweise exportiert, wenn seine Raffinerien nicht angegriffen werden.
Der größte Gewinner des Diesel-Abkommens ist Russland. Seit Monaten bemüht sich Putin, den von den USA gemeinsam mit Israel begonnenen Iran-Krieg für seine Zwecke zu nutzen und hat sich mehrfach als Vermittler ins Spiel gebracht. Zudem nutzte er die aus dem Krieg erwachsenen Preissprünge beim Diesel um eine Lockerung der Sanktionen gegen Russland zu erwirken.
Nun bringt der Deal das Regime wieder ein Stück weiter auf die Weltbühne - wie schon das Treffen von Trump und Putin in Anchorage im vergangenen Jahr oder zuletzt die Einladung Trump zum G20-Gipfel in den USA.

title: Axios: Під "енергетичним перемир'ям" Трамп мав на увазі лише припинення атак на НПЗ
content_c:
Axios: Під "енергетичним перемир'ям" Трамп мав на увазі лише припинення атак на НПЗ
Представник Білого дому заявив у коментарі Axios, що "енергетичне перемир'я" в розумінні президента США Дональда Трампа означає, що Росія та Україна припинять атаки лише на нафтопереробні заводи один одного, і саме цього очікують від України. Водночас в Україні є лише один НПЗ, який не працює на повну потужність.
Джерело: Axios із посиланням на джерела
Дослівно: "У неділю президент Трамп оголосив про "енергетичне перемир'я" між Росією та Україною, маючи на увазі потенційну угоду, згідно з якою кожна зі сторін припинить атаки на нафтопереробні заводи, – і він очікує, що Володимир Зеленський дотримуватиметься її, повідомив представник Білого дому.
Представник зазначив, що якщо атаки на нафтопереробні заводи припиняться, наступним кроком може стати угода про припинення ударів по електростанціях та енергетичних мережах".
Деталі: Як зазначає видання, пропозиція "нафтопереробний завод за нафтопереробний завод", як її назвав представник Білого дому, є нерівноцінною.
Український чиновник повідомив Axios, що в країні є лише один нафтопереробний завод, який росіяни неодноразово атакували і який не працює на повну потужність. Натомість Росія має розгалужену мережу нафтопереробних заводів.
"Ми імпортуємо дизельне паливо та газ. Нам потрібно, щоб росіяни припинили атакувати нашу електромережу", – сказав український чиновник.
"Росіяни думають над цим. Скоро ми дізнаємося, чи готові вони до цього", – зазначив представник Білого дому.
Як пише видання, представники Білого дому попереджають, що атаки України на російські нафтопереробні заводи завдають більшої шкоди відносинам Зеленського з Трампом, ніж самій Росії.
"Трамп справді розлючений. Він вважає, що Зеленський сприймає допомогу США як належне", – сказав представник Білого дому.
Повідомляється також, що на тлі кризи з Україною посланці президента США Стів Віткофф і Джаред Кушнер відклали заплановану поїздку до Москви, "принаймні доти, доки не з'ясується, чи готові Україна та європейські країни погодитися на нову узгоджену пропозицію для Путіна".
Передісторія:
- Президент США Дональд Трамп 11 жовтня заявив, що Україна та Росія нібито погодилися на негайне енергетичне перемир'я.
- Журналіст Axios Барак Равід заявив, що Зеленський не знав про оголошення "енергетичного перемир'я" між Україною та РФ, про яке заявив Трамп, але готовий погодитися на це.
- Згодом Зеленський повідомив, що вже після заяви Трампа росіяни завдали удару по ТЕЦ-5 у Харкові, а також по електростанції в Києві.
- Російська сторона досі не коментувала заяву Трампа про "перемир'я".
- Водночас міністр закордонних справ України Андрій Сибіга заявив, що Росія порушила "енергетичне перемир'я" одразу після його оголошення Трампом.
description: Представник Білого дому пояснив, що пропозиція США стосується припинення атак на нафтопереробні заводи обох країн. Деталі – в матеріалі.

"Росіяни думають над цим. Скоро ми дізнаємося, чи готові вони до цього", – зазначив представник Білого дому.
Як пише видання, представники Білого дому попереджають, що атаки України на російські нафтопереробні заводи завдають більшої шкоди відносинам Зеленського з Трампом, ніж самій Росії.
"Трамп справді розлючений. Він вважає, що Зеленський сприймає допомогу США як належне", – сказав представник Білого дому.
Повідомляється також, що на тлі кризи з Україною посланці президента США Стів Віткофф і Джаред Кушнер відклали заплановану поїздку до Москви, "принаймні доти, доки не з'ясується, чи готові Україна та європейські країни погодитися на нову узгоджену пропозицію для Путіна".
Передісторія:
- Президент США Дональд Трамп 11 жовтня заявив, що Україна та Росія нібито погодилися на негайне енергетичне перемир'я.
- Журналіст Axios Барак Равід заявив, що Зеленський не знав про оголошення "енергетичного перемир'я" між Україною та РФ, про яке заявив Трамп, але готовий погодитися на це.
- Згодом Зеленський повідомив, що вже після заяви Трампа росіяни завдали удару по ТЕЦ-5 у Харкові, а також по електростанції в Києві.
- Російська сторона досі не коментувала заяву Трампа про "перемир'я".
- Водночас міністр закордонних справ України Андрій Сибіга заявив, що Росія порушила "енергетичне перемир'я" одразу після його оголошення Трампом.

title: Данія та Німеччина вже зробили свій вибір: у НАТО пояснили, як провалити план Кремля в Україні
content_c:
Данія та Німеччина вже зробили свій вибір: у НАТО пояснили, як провалити план Кремля в Україні
Посилення допомоги Україні допоможе продемонструвати Москві, що її спроби залякати західних союзників не досягають мети.
Європейським державам варто посилити підтримку України у відповідь на російські гібридні атаки проти країн континенту.
Про це заявив верховний головнокомандувач Об’єднаних збройних сил НАТО в Європі генерал Алексус Гринкевич, повідомляє Bloomberg.
За словами генерала, Росія активізує агресивні дії проти європейських держав. Серед них — порушення повітряного простору країн НАТО, підпали, диверсії та кібератаки.
«Вони намагаються зламати нашу спільну волю», — наголосив Гринкевич під час Варшавського безпекового форуму 11 жовтня.
Як приклад ефективної реакції на такі загрози генерал навів Данію та Німеччину. Після гібридних атак на їхній території ці країни збільшили допомогу Україні.
На думку командувача, така позиція є правильною, оскільки демонструє Росії, що тиск на європейських союзників не допоможе їй досягти поставлених цілей.
«Це належні відповіді, які показують Росії, що цілей, яких вона прагне досягти, досягнути неможливо», — пояснив Гринкевич.
Він також звернув увагу, що російські гібридні операції тривають на тлі значних втрат, яких армія РФ зазнає у війні проти України.
Водночас українські військові посилюють економічний тиск на Росію, завдаючи ударів по нафтопереробних заводах і центрах обробки даних, розташованих у глибині російської території.
НАТО переважно залишає за окремими державами право самостійно визначати реакцію на подібні інциденти. Водночас Гринкевич заявив, що готовий публічно називати відповідальних за такі дії, якщо відповідна країна звернеться до нього.
Окремо генерал визнав, що в Європі набирають популярності політичні сили, які виступають проти подальшої допомоги Україні. Додатковим випробуванням для прихильників підтримки Києва стануть вибори, заплановані в низці європейських країн у 2027 році.
Попри це, Гринкевич переконаний, що стратегічне значення України для безпеки Європи переважить політичні розбіжності. Він вважає, що навіть ті, хто нині сумнівається в доцільності допомоги Києву, згодом усвідомлять її важливість для захисту власних держав.
«Думаю, їм дуже швидко стане цілком очевидно, що правильно робити і чому це необхідно для їхньої власної національної безпеки», — зазначив генерал.
Під час візиту до Польщі Гринкевич також представляє підходи Альянсу до забезпечення швидкої перемоги над Росією в разі її нападу на територію НАТО.
За словами командувача, оприлюднення так званої «теорії перемоги» має посилити стримування Москви. Росія повинна чітко розуміти, з якими наслідками зіткнеться в разі спроби захопити територію однієї з держав Альянсу.
Запропонований підхід передбачає поєднання безпілотників і технологій штучного інтелекту з уже наявними військовими перевагами НАТО. Зокрема, Гринкевич наголосив на ролі винищувачів F-35.
Водночас генерал підкреслив, що за появи відповідних можливостей необхідно використовувати шанси для дипломатичного врегулювання російсько-української війни.
Раніше повідомлялося, що Москва може використовувати дрони, кібератаки, диверсії та дезінформацію, щоб перевірити готовність НАТО реагувати на загрози.
Ми раніше інформували, що Росія розраховує, що європейські країни не зможуть тривалий час протистояти її намірам продовжувати війну проти України.

title: Зеленский ввел санкции против производителей «Искандеров» и «Цирконов»: кого ещё включили в списки
content_c:
Президент Владимир Зеленский ввел в действие решение СНБО о введении санкций против субъектов в РФ, причастных к производству баллистического оружия, а также отдельно против лиц, действующих в интересах врага на временно оккупированных территориях.
В частности, первый пакет санкций применен в отношении 70 лиц, причастных к производству баллистических ракет «Искандер-М» и «Циркон». Речь идет о ключевых сотрудниках предприятий российского ОПК и химической отрасли, участвующих в организации непрерывного промышленного цикла по производству баллистического оружия: предприятия «Авиатек», «Авангард», «Алтай», «Азот», заводы «Салют», «Стрела», «ВНИИР-Прогресс», «Машиностроитель», Воткинский завод и Институт машиностроения имени В. В. Бахирева и другие.
«Предприятия, производящие “Искандеры” и “Цирконы”, уже давно находятся под санкциями Украины и большинства партнеров. Но ракеты собирают конкретные люди: инженеры, технологи, руководители производства. Теперь мы вносим в санкционный список и их — 70 ключевых работников ракетной цепочки, от химических заводов, поставляющих компоненты топлива и взрывчатки, до сборочных цехов Воткинска. Каждый, кто производит ракеты для ударов по украинским городам, должен понимать: ответственность личная, и она не минует», – подчеркнул уполномоченный президента по вопросам санкционной политики Владислав Власюк.
В санкционном пакете, касающемся лиц, помогающих России обходить санкции в финансовой сфере, 28 физических и 27 юридических лиц. Среди них компании — операторы криптобирж, сервисы обмена криптовалют, их руководители и владельцы. Ограничения также введены в отношении руководителей и владельцев компаний, входящих в теневую банковскую сеть A7 и публично предлагающих инструменты обхода финансовых санкций.
Еще одним решением санкции применены против 10 физических и 21 юридического лица, а также против двух морских судов, которые являются пособниками России и действуют в ее интересах на временно оккупированных территориях Украины.
Напомним, 7 октября 2026 года послы стран Евросоюза согласовали внесение в санкционные списки 743 физических лиц и 826 юридических лиц, связанных с российским военно-промышленным комплексом.
description: Решения предусматривают введение ограничений в отношении участников ракетного производства, теневых финансовых сетей, а также лиц и компаний, действующих в интересах РФ.

В. Бахирева и другие.
«Предприятия, производящие “Искандеры” и “Цирконы”, уже давно находятся под санкциями Украины и большинства партнеров. Но ракеты собирают конкретные люди: инженеры, технологи, руководители производства. Теперь мы вносим в санкционный список и их — 70 ключевых работников ракетной цепочки, от химических заводов, поставляющих компоненты топлива и взрывчатки, до сборочных цехов Воткинска. Каждый, кто производит ракеты для ударов по украинским городам, должен понимать: ответственность личная, и она не минует», – подчеркнул уполномоченный президента по вопросам санкционной политики Владислав Власюк.
В санкционном пакете, касающемся лиц, помогающих России обходить санкции в финансовой сфере, 28 физических и 27 юридических лиц. Среди них компании — операторы криптобирж, сервисы обмена криптовалют, их руководители и владельцы. Ограничения также введены в отношении руководителей и владельцев компаний, входящих в теневую банковскую сеть A7 и публично предлагающих инструменты обхода финансовых санкций.
Еще одним решением санкции применены против 10 физических и 21 юридического лица, а также против двух морских судов, которые являются пособниками России и действуют в ее интересах на временно оккупированных территориях Украины.
Напомним, 7 октября 2026 года послы стран Евросоюза согласовали внесение в санкционные списки 743 физических лиц и 826 юридических лиц, связанных с российским военно-промышленным комплексом.

title: Кількість загиблих унаслідок атаки на Івано-Франківськ зросла до трьох – мер
content_c:
Кількість загиблих унаслідок російської атаки на Івано-Франківськ у неділю зросла до трьох, ще одна людина поранена, повідомив міський голова Руслан Марцінків.
"Наші служби працюють на місці. Допоможемо закрити вибиті вікна. Відзавтра постраждалі мешканці та підприємці зможуть подавати заяви на допомогу в ЦНАПі", – написав він у телеграмі.
За словами мера, внаслідок атаки також пошкоджено цивільну інфраструктуру. На оприлюднених фото видно пошкоджене приміщення пекарні-магазину з вибитими вікнами.
Марцінків закликав містян реагувати на повітряну тривогу та не перебувати під час неї на вулиці.
Раніше повідомлялося про дві жертви.

title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
content_c:
Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
content_c:
A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.
An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.
The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.
In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.
After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”
The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.
The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.
Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.
On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”
On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.
The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.
Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.
The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.
Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.
It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.
Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.
Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.
The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.
The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”
The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.
The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.
Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.
The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.
Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.
Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

title: Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?
content_c:
Surrogacy in Georgia is booming, but at what cost?
October 11, 2026
Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect the their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts.
Olga is a German citizen, but was born and raised in Russia. That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia. So, Olga and Daniel traveled there.
Georgia new destination for surrogate mothers
In recent years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children.
Since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023.
Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment.
Anastasia said she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted, and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant.
"I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She said she's ready to become a surrogate mother again.
Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in Tbilisi or Batumi are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge.
Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example.
Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand
Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers."
Both work in the medical field, and Olga said perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she said. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga added.
In the spring of 2024, the couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment.
"They had initially told us that the surrogate would spent the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel told DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war."
Human rights experts criticize legislation
Georgian laws have a weak spot, human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze told DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents and the clinics, but they don't consider the roles that agencies play.
In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the involved parties. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms.
After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition, say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination.
Agencies guided by material interests
"Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya, an anthropologist studying reproduction and migration at the University of Leeds, told DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents."
Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," said Olga.
And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga said. "I felt like I was being manipulated."
The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now.
Mark Sheider and Asja Lokina contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Russian.
